implementation_notes: The standard library ships the pattern: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n) owns the worker threads and the queue, submit() returns a Future, map() and as_completed() cover the batch shapes, and using the executor as a context manager joins the workers on exit. The Future-based interface is what replaces the classic structure - no Thread objects, no queue, no locks. The GIL means a thread pool parallelises waiting (I/O, subprocesses, ctypes/numpy releases), not pure-Python CPU work, for which ProcessPoolExecutor (or 3.14's InterpreterPoolExecutor with per-interpreter GILs) is the right pool; on free-threaded builds the CPU-bound caveat weakens. Since 3.13 max_workers defaults to min(32, os.process_cpu_count() + 4).
pitfalls: A worker that waits on another Future of the same pool deadlocks once the pool is saturated (the docs demonstrate both variants).
Threads are joined at interpreter exit before atexit handlers run, so long-running tasks block shutdown and teardown may never execute.
Exceptions live inside the Future and vanish silently if result() is never called; contextvars do not follow a task onto whichever thread picks it up.

variants.name: Hand-rolled threading.Thread + queue.Queue pool
variants.idiom_name: threading.Thread workers over queue.Queue with task_done/join
variants.implementation_notes: The pool can be written directly on threading.Thread and queue.Queue: N workers loop on Queue.get(), run the callable and call queue.task_done(), while queue.join() waits for the backlog and one sentinel per worker ends the loop; a maxsize gives put() blocking backpressure (and Queue.shutdown() exists since 3.13 for a hard stop). queue.Queue is the piece that replaces the mutex/condition-variable pair, and PriorityQueue or LifoQueue substitutes a different queue policy. Keep this form when a custom policy is needed or an old interpreter has no concurrent.futures; otherwise the stdlib executor already implements it correctly, including futures and shutdown.
pitfalls: Forgetting task_done() makes queue.join() hang forever, and calling it too often raises ValueError.
daemon=True hides an unclean shutdown: threads die mid-task at interpreter exit unless joined explicitly.
With the GIL, tasks smaller than the queue hand-off cost make the pool slower than a plain loop.
